Neonatal specimens of the common guitarfish (Rhinobatos rhinobatos) emerge from their mothers at a total length of 25.7 centimeters [Lb = 25.7 centimeters], a dimension that reflects the constraints of yolk-dependent gestation within a viviparous reproductive mode. This length at birth is relatively modest compared to the ultimate size the species can achieve, and the corresponding wet weight at birth has been estimated at 48.5 grams [Wwb = 48.5 grams] based on a cubic scaling relationship with adult length. The gestation period itself, during which the developing embryos rely entirely on yolk reserves, extends for approximately 9 months under typical thermal conditions. At a water temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], the age at birth has been recorded as 274.5 days [ab = 274.5 days], a duration that synchronizes parturition with favorable seasonal conditions for neonatal survival in shallow coastal nursery habitats.

Field surveys and long-term mark-recapture studies have documented that adult common guitarfish can attain a considerable ultimate total length of 147 centimeters [Li = 147 centimeters], placing this species among the larger members of the Rhinobatidae family in the Mediterranean and eastern Atlantic. This maximum recorded size is reached only after a prolonged growth period characterized by asymptotic deceleration in somatic expansion. The species also exhibits a clear size threshold for the onset of gonadal maturation; examination of reproductive tracts from fishery-dependent samples indicates that sexual maturity is attained at a total length of approximately 67 centimeters [Lp = approximately 67 centimeters]. This length at puberty corresponds to a phase when individuals have accumulated sufficient energy reserves to transition from exclusive investment in somatic growth toward the energetic demands of gametogenesis and reproductive pairing.

Reproductive output in Rhinobatos rhinobatos is characterized by moderate fecundity and relatively infrequent breeding events. Under the stable thermal regime of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], females typically produce litters containing between 4 and 10 pups per reproductive event [N_R_i = between 4 and 10 pups per reproductive event], a litter size that aligns with the matrotrophic histotrophy strategy common to many rhinobatids. Furthermore, the frequency of these reproductive events is constrained by the energetic recovery period following parturition, with mature females capable of producing approximately one litter per year [F_R_i = approximately one litter per year] in optimal conditions. This combination of modest litter size and annual reproductive frequency yields a sustainable recruitment rate that is comparatively low relative to more fecund elasmobranchs, underscoring the species' vulnerability to overexploitation.

The demographic schedule of the common guitarfish features a notably slow pace of life, with key life-history transitions spread across several years. In the Mediterranean basin, where ambient seawater temperatures average around 15 °C [T = 15 °C], the age at which individuals achieve their first successful reproduction has been estimated at 5 years [tR = 5 years]. This protracted delay in the onset of breeding reflects the substantial time required to accumulate the necessary somatic reserves and to complete the morphological development of reproductive organs. Additionally, the species' maximum recorded longevity under natural conditions has been documented at 7 years [am = 7 years] at 15 °C [T = 15 °C], indicating that the entire post-pubertal reproductive window spans only a relatively short interval of approximately two years for most individuals, further limiting lifetime reproductive potential.

Comparative analyses with other rhinobatid species reveal that the life-history strategy of Rhinobatos rhinobatos is consistent with a K-selected demographic profile typical of many coastal elasmobranchs. The relatively large body size at birth, estimated at 25.7 centimeters [Lb = 25.7 centimeters] total length, and the considerable mass of approximately 48.5 grams [Wwb = approximately 48.5 grams] at parturition, provide neonates with a size advantage against gape-limited predators. The attainment of reproductive maturity at about 67 centimeters [Lp = about 67 centimeters] total length marks a critical developmental milestone after which females begin to allocate resources toward gestation. Under the prevailing thermal conditions of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], the 7-year lifespan (7 years) [am = 7 years] represents a moderate longevity for a batoid of this body size, while the average production of one litter per year [F_R_i = one litter per year] containing 4 to 10 pups [N_R_i = containing 4 to 10 pups] underscores the species' limited capacity for rapid population recovery.
